scores.claim_text: F-35 is Hexcel's largest S&D program, <25% of S&D revenues.
supports: pentagon_jbook returned 2 matched PEs for 'F-35' (F-35 C2D2 PE 0604840F; F-35 Squadrons PE 0207142F) but BOTH yielded NOT_FOUND_IN_TIMERANGE for the 2023 cutoff — the corpus is FY2026 R-2/P-40 exhibits, which do not contain pre-cutoff historical funding rows.

Contractor-level lookup 'Lockheed Martin' returned SDA Transport Layer programs (Tranche 3 UNFUNDED_TWO_PLUS_YEARS, T0-2 FUNDED_SHRINKING, T3 Tracking Layer FUNDED_STEADY) — orthogonal to F-35 and not informative for Hexcel's F-35 exposure.

usaspending.query_dod_contracts shows 83 awards / $8.6M total to Hexcel Corp / Hexcel Corporation / ARC Technologies LLC (a Hexcel sub) — confirms Hexcel is a real DoD vendor, but contracts are sub-tier (radar camouflage units, DLA fiber-reinforcing material, EMERGENT IV BAA proposals) and do NOT identify a Hexcel F-35 contract line.
scores.interpretation: Hexcel is a Tier-2 composites supplier; it sells materials INTO Lockheed Martin's F-35 supply chain rather than holding a PE-level prime contract. The J-Book corpus does not contain pre-2023 funding rows, so the FY2021-base 'largest program' claim cannot be verified or falsified from the FY26 corpus. The corpus-coverage gap rule applies (heuristic #1: NOT_FOUND/NOT_FOUND_IN_TIMERANGE → UNVERIFIABLE; #7: do not penalize NOT_FOUND). Note: at 2023-01-15 cutoff, F-35 was a steady-state production program with multi-year LRIP/Lot procurement; framework would have read the claim as benign.

scores.claim_text: Bell-Boeing V-22 Osprey is one of Hexcel's two largest blade programs.
supports: pentagon_jbook returned NOT_FOUND for both 'V-22 Osprey' and 'V-22' — corpus does not cover V-22 procurement P-40 lines.
Heuristic #7 explicitly states NOT_FOUND is not a red flag; v1 corpus focuses on RDT&E/Procurement PEs not legacy rotorcraft.
Materially, V-22 procurement was already in tail-down mode by 2023 cutoff (multi-year contract MV-22B Lot 17 had been awarded); this is platform-level information, not a Hexcel-specific divergence.
scores.interpretation: Corpus coverage gap, not an underdelivery signal. Hexcel sells blade materials into the V-22 supply chain via Bell/Boeing; this is a sub-tier exposure that is not directly J-Book-mappable to a single PE.

scores.claim_text: UH-60 Black Hawk wide-chord blade program is one of Hexcel's two largest blade programs.
supports: pentagon_jbook returned NOT_FOUND for 'UH-60 Black Hawk'.
UH-60M procurement is in Army Aircraft Procurement (P-40 line) which is not in the v1 corpus.
Hexcel is again at the materials layer, supplying Sikorsky (LMT subsidiary).
scores.interpretation: Coverage gap rule applies (heuristic #7). UH-60M was on a multi-year-X contract (MYP IX, FY22-26) signed 2022; rate was steady to declining at the time but the claim is sub-tier.

scores.claim_text: CH-53K King Stallion is a future growth program for Hexcel (composite blades + new helicopter programs in prototype).
supports: pentagon_jbook returned NOT_FOUND for 'CH-53K'.
CH-53K is in Navy Aircraft Procurement (P-40) plus a small remaining RDT&E tail; not in v1 corpus.
Forward language ('future growth', 'prototypes') is exactly the J-Book-grounded pipeline-language pattern the rubric flags, but corpus cannot adjudicate it.
scores.interpretation: If corpus did cover Navy P-40 lines, this would be a primary verification target because the company is asserting forward growth dependence. Recommend extending programs.json. Until then, UNVERIFIABLE per heuristic #7. Note: CH-53K Lot 5 procurement was on track at the 2023-01-15 cutoff, so even with coverage the score would likely have been PASS or MODERATE at worst (price/performance issues, not funding).

scores.claim_text: Hexcel is qualified to supply Airbus A400M military transport.
supports: pentagon_jbook returned NOT_FOUND — A400M is a European OCCAR program, outside DoD J-Book scope by design.
Heuristic #7 explicitly notes corpus does not cover every J-Book line worldwide and that European/foreign programs would be expected misses.
scores.interpretation: Out-of-scope for Pentagon J-Book by definition. Not a red flag. The claim is also a qualification statement, not a forward-revenue assertion, so materiality is low (heuristic #2).

scores.claim_text: Government-funded space launch (solid rocket booster cases, fairings, payload doors) and satellite buses/solar arrays are continuing demand sources; sales depend on what is funded.
supports: pentagon_jbook matched 'Space Launch' to 'National Security Space Launch Program' PE 1206853SF (Space Force) — but with NOT_FOUND_IN_TIMERANGE for 2023 cutoff (corpus is FY26 only).
The PE that DID match has no UNFUNDED status declared (status_declared=null), no replacement_program, no earmark flag. There is no negative forward signal.
Solid Rocket Motor query returned NOT_FOUND.

Importantly, Hexcel itself flags 'sales are dependent upon those that are funded and the extent of the funding' — i.e., the filing PRE-DISCLOSES the funding-dependency risk. This is the opposite of the J-Book divergence pattern.
scores.M_value: NOT_FOUND_IN_TIMERANGE (matched PE 1206853SF NSSL, no negative status)
scores.interpretation: Hexcel's space narrative is generic and self-hedged; there is no specific PE-revenue tied to a vanishing line. The company already disclosed that 2021 Space sales DECLINED 3.0%. Pre-disclosure of weakness defeats the divergence-pattern thesis. PASS per heuristic #1 (no negative J-Book signal) and heuristic #2 (low materiality — language is qualitative).

scores.claim_text: No S&D program other than F-35 is >10% of S&D revenue; portfolio is diversified across many named platforms.
supports: pentagon_jbook contractor lookup for 'Hexcel' returned NOT_FOUND — corpus does not index Hexcel as a primary contractor on any seeded PE (it is in fact a Tier-2/3 supplier).

usaspending corroborates Tier-2 status: $8.6M total DoD obligations across 83 awards is trivial vs Hexcel's FY2021 ~$1.3B revenue; the company is NOT primarily a federal-contract revenue entity, it sells through Airbus/Boeing/Lockheed/Sikorsky/Bell.
The 'no program >10% (ex-F-35)' diversification claim is the OPPOSITE of the canonical concentration pattern this cohort targets.
scores.interpretation: Diversification claim is structurally consistent with Hexcel's business model (materials supplier across many platforms). The J-Book divergence pattern targets small-caps with concentrated PE exposure — Hexcel is the inverse case. PASS.

scores.claim_text: Top-2 customers (Airbus and Boeing) and their subcontractors are 49% of 2021 net sales (down from 64% in 2019); Airbus 33% (29% CA + 4% S&D), Boeing 16% (12% CA + 4% S&D).
supports: edgar_fts.query_fulltext(search_term='Hexcel', cik=0000936468) → 0 hits in Lockheed Martin filings since 2018.
edgar_fts.query_fulltext(search_term='Hexcel', cik=0000012927) → 0 hits in Boeing filings since 2018.

Counterparty non-mention is EXPECTED — neither Boeing nor Lockheed individually discloses Hexcel as a material supplier, which is consistent with Tier-2 status. This is a NULL counterparty signal, not a divergence.
The customer-concentration trend (64%→52%→49%) is moving in the correct direction (diversifying).
scores.M_value: 0 hits each — Tier-2 supplier invisibility, expected
scores.interpretation: Counterparty-disclosure null is structurally expected for a sub-tier materials supplier; not informative for the J-Book divergence pattern. Concentration is also DECLINING, which weakens any 'top-customer dependency' thesis. PASS.

scores.claim_text: Hexcel increased PAN and carbon-fiber capacity to serve aerospace demand; a new production line can take up to a year to qualify.

No M-source in catalog directly verifies 'capacity expansion in recent years' for a specific product line.

scores.interpretation: Operational claim outside the J-Book divergence frame; not verifiable from available M-sources. UNVERIFIABLE.

summary.framework_diagnosis: HEXCEL IS A NEGATIVE CONTROL FOR THE J-BOOK DIVERGENCE PATTERN. The canonical YSS/IONQ pattern requires (a) small-cap with (b) concentrated revenue from (c) a named Program Element that (d) the J-Book has zeroed. Hexcel violates all four prongs: it is mid-cap ~$1.3B revenue, top-program concentration is bounded (<25% of S&D = <8% of total), it names platforms (F-35, V-22, UH-60, CH-53K) NOT Program Elements, and customer concentration is DECLINING. The framework correctly does NOT fire any severity flags. The 5 NOT_FOUND results reflect (i) corpus coverage gaps for legacy rotorcraft P-40 lines (V-22, UH-60, CH-53K) and (ii) out-of-scope European programs (A400M). The 2 NOT_FOUND_IN_TIMERANGE results (F-35, NSSL) reflect FY26-only corpus vs 2023 cutoff. CONCLUSION: framework would not have generated a short signal on HXL at 2023-01-15, which is appropriate — Hexcel's risks (Boeing 787 production cuts, COVID-19 widebody hangover, wind-energy attrition) are commercial-aerospace + industrial, not Pentagon-program divergence.
